title: 120 Effect of copper oxide wire particles on parasitism and growth in Katahdin lambs divergently selected for fecal egg count estimated breeding value: Year 2
content:
Abstract
Gastrointestinal nematodes (GIN) are a major threat to small ruminant production, especially as anthelmintic resistance continues to rise. Multiple tools, such as copper oxide wire particles (COWP) and genetic selection, should be utilized to support an integrated parasite management plan to mitigate effects of GIN infection. The objective of this project was to determine the interaction of COWP and genetic selection for fecal egg count (FEC) estimated breeding value (EBV) on GIN infection and performance in Katahdin lambs. Spring-born Katahdin ram lambs (n = 39) selected for extremely high FEC EBV (HFEC, PFEC EBV = +129%) or low FEC EBV (LFEC, PFEC EBV = -81%), were managed as one contemporary group on fescue-based pasture at the Southwest Virginia Agricultural Research and Extension Center (Glade Spring, VA). Lambs were three-way dewormed at weaning (June 13) and rested for 34 days. At the start of the project (July 17, Week 0) all lambs were dosed with 5,000 L3 Haemonchus contortus (Hc). Packed cell volume, FEC, FAMACHA scores, and body weights were collected bi-weekly for 16 weeks. A random subset of lambs (HFEC-COWP, n = 10; LFEC-COWP, n =10) were given a 2 g COWP bolus at weeks 4, 8, and 12, while an equal number of remaining lambs were managed as the control (HFEC-Con, n = 9; LFEC-Con, n = 10). Additional fecal samples were collected on weeks 4, 8, and 12 for larval identification via coproculture. Deworming was determined based on FAMACHA ≥ 3. Statistical analyses were performed using PROC Mixed Procedure of SAS (SAS Institute, Cary, NC) and FEC data were log transformed for normality. There was no effect of COWP treatment on FEC (P = 0.13). Lambs treated with COWP had lower PCV compared to lambs not treated (29.1% vs. 30.7%, respectively; P < 0.05). Copper oxide wire particle treatment had no effect on FAMACHA score (P = 0.38) or overall ADG (P = 0.78). LFEC-selected lambs had lower FEC than HFEC-selected lambs (1015 vs. 1853 eggs/g, respectively; P < 0.01). However, FEC EBV genotype had no effect on FAMACHA score, PCV or overall ADG (P = 0.35, P = 0.52 and P = 0.42, respectively). Deworming was required for 30% of HFEC-Con lambs and 20% of the LFEC-COWP lambs. Coproculture results indicate 5% Hc larvae in all treatment groups. Despite multiple treatments with COWP, infection level was not changed. However, this lack of efficacy may have been a result of a relatively low proportion of Hc present in lambs. Selection for low FEC, regardless of COWP treatment, can lessen parasite burden. Additional parasite management tools should be considered along with genetic selection to control parasite burden in small ruminants and COWP may offer benefits in higher Hc environments.
